title: Pregnancy Complicated by Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: 17 Pregnancy Complicated by Diabetes Mellitus
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Diabetes mellitus that results from relative or absolute lack of insulin is encountered during pregnancy in two situations: pregestational diabetes mellitus (pre-GDM) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The former refers to women who had diabetes mellitus prior to conception, with microvascular diabetes-associated complications (renal, retinal, cardiac, and nervous system), and the latter refers to otherwise healthy women who developed glucose intolerance during the index pregnancy. These two entities are entirely distinct from both obstetric and neonatal perspectives. Pre-GDM and its associated small vessel injury may affect placental function and fetal growth, whereas GDM is a transient problem that affects the fetus in the opposite way (i.e., macrosomia and its obstetrical consequences—dystocia and increased incidence of operative delivery). This chapter focuses mainly on GDM and its neonatal consequences.
paragraphs.heading: MAYA RAM WEINER, POLINA GUREVICH, ERIC S. SHINWELL, AND YARIV YOGEV

paragraphs.text: GDM is one of the most common pregnancy complications. GDM is a state of carbohydrate intolerance that is defined as any degree of hyperglycemia that is recognized for the first time during pregnancy.1 The prevalence of GDM has been increasing over time, generally in parallel with the prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D), possibly due to the increasing rates of obesity in the general population and the trend toward advanced maternal age in pregnancy.2,3 The prevalence has increased by more than 30% in the last two decades3 and is now estimated to affect between 7% and more than 30% of all pregnancies worldwide.3,4 Differences in the geographic location, ethnic groups, and characteristics of the population screened and the diagnostic criteria that are applied are responsible for the wide reported range.3–5 Moreover, and of greater concern, a diagnosis of GDM identifies approximately 80% of these mothers who subsequently develop overt T2D and metabolic syndrome.6 Furthermore, their offspring are also at higher risk for future
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: T2D, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and future cardiovascular diseases.7
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: The screening and diagnosis of GDM have a long history of controversy, related mainly to significant implications on health care costs, the effect on obstetric interventions, and whether diagnosis and treatment of GDM will improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. In earlier times, it was common for screening for GDM to be based on the patient’s medical history, focusing on past obstetric outcomes such as bearing a child with macrosomia, and family history of T2D. Those high-risk women underwent a 3-hour, 100-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), and a diagnosis of GDM was established when two or more of the four glucose values met or exceeded threshold levels.1,8 Screening for GDM based on risk factors rather than universal screening was thought to be cost effective and, more importantly, reduced the burden of unnecessary OGTTs in low-risk women. In practice, this approach has complicated the detection process and failed to identify half of the women with GDM who did not have any risk factors.9,10 Realizing the insensitivity of the selective screening, it was suggested first by O’Sullivan et al. in 1973 and later adopted by the US Preventive Services Task Force11 to screen all pregnant women for GDM by a non-fasting, 1-hour, 50-g glucose challenge test (GCT) at or beyond 24 gestational weeks.8 They recommended that only pregnant women who did not pass the GCT should proceed to the second-step, 100-g, 3-hour OGTT for definitive diagnosis.
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Consecutive studies suggested that lesser degrees of hyperglycemia are also associated with an increased risk of adverse perinatal outcome, including large for gestational age (LGA) fetuses, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia, cesarean delivery, and hypertensive disorders. Consequently, in 1999, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that a GDM diagnosis should be made similar to
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: that for the detection of T2D, and a 2-hour, 75-g OGTT test should be applied instead of the former 3-hour, 100-g OGTT. These criteria were not evidence based, as their cutoff values were selected arbitrarily by expert opinion and consensus.12 However, the validity of this test as a screening tool was supported after being used in the Hyperglycemia and Adverse Pregnancy Outcome (HAPO) study in 2008. It was a large, multicenter observational study designed to examine the relationship between maternal hyperglycemia less severe than overt GDM and adverse pregnancy outcome. They determined maternal glucose levels at 24 to 32 weeks of gestation by a 2-hour, 75-g OGTT and reported that all three maternal plasma glucose values (fasting, 1 hour, and 2 hours) correlated with adverse outcomes. This study clearly demonstrated a relationship between increased maternal blood glucose and birth weight, cord blood C-peptide (a measure for intrauterine fetal hyperinsulinemia), neonatal hypoglycemia, and delivery by cesarean section.
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The evidence provided by the HAPO study formed the basis of the International Association of Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) criteria for GDM screening and diagnosis in 2010.13 The IADPSG recommended a one-step method involving a 2-hour, 75-g oral OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks of gestation and proposed that only one
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: value needs to be abnormal in order to diagnose GDM. The implementation of these guidelines would presumably double the number of patients diagnosed with GDM, but no evidence exists that this will lead to clinically significant improvement in maternal and neonatal outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Regardless of these reservations, universal screening for GDM was adopted by more than 90% of practices that perform the sequential two-step testing and is recommended by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines.1 Thus a 50-g GCT is performed in all pregnant women between 24 and 28 weeks’ gestation. Screening cutoff values are 130 mg/dL (7.20 mmol/L; 90% sensitivity) or 140 mg/dL (7.75 mmol/L; 80% sensitivity). In women who screen positive, a 3-hour, 100-g OGTT is used to diagnose GDM. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed if two or more plasma glucose measurements are abnormal. On the other hand, the WHO recommends simultaneous screening and diagnosis using a 75-g OGTT, and the American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends either approach (Table 17.1).
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Early pregnancy screening for undiagnosed T2D is suggested for women with diabetic risk factors (glycosuria, diabetes in a first-degree relative, history of glucose intolerance, previous GDM, obesity, and a previous infant with macrosomia). At-risk women should be screened at their first prenatal
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: visit. The best test for early screening is not clear and may include the non-pregnancy recommended screening tests: fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 75-g OGTT, random plasma glucose, and HbA1C, or the typical 24- to 28-week GDM diagnostic tests (50-g GCT followed by OGTT). It is of note that testing for FPG or HbA1C could lead to underdiagnosis in women with pre-existing diabetes, as they both decrease early in pregnancy and the typical 24- to 28-week diagnostic testing has not been validated for diagnosis in early pregnancy.14 It was found that a large proportion of women who had negative early pregnancy screening developed GDM; therefore GDM screening should be repeated between 24 and 28 weeks in women found negative in early pregnancy diabetic testing.1 The interested reader will find more information about the controversial diagnosis of GDM elsewhere.15,16
paragraphs.heading: Screening and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Despite uncertainty regarding the clinical value of treating GDM, data strongly suggest that treatment may reduce adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Evidence of possible adverse effects associated with even mild maternal hyperglycemia comes from the HAPO trial.17,18 The results of this trial point to a linear correlation between increasing maternal glucose levels and increasing birth weight, primary cesarean delivery, fetal C-peptide levels, neonatal hypoglycemia, and long-term effects including higher risk of developing T2D and children with a higher risk of obesity and increased body fat. Most clinicians use glucose targets as defined by the Fifth International Workshop-Conference on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (Table 17.2).
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Management

paragraphs.text: “Diabesity” is a relatively new term denoting the combination of diabetes and obesity. In a large population-based study, Blickstein et al.19 found that the ill-effect of pregravid obesity is greater than that of GDM. Obesity, with and without GDM, increased the odds of having chronic hypertension, whereas preeclampsia appeared to be influenced by obesity only, as were the risk of births at <33 weeks’ gestation, of birth weight >4000 g, low 5-minute Apgar scores, and neonatal intensive care unit admissions. They concluded that obesity (without diabetes) is more frequently associated with adverse perinatal outcomes than GDM in nonobese mothers. They argued that a campaign to decrease pregravid obesity should have at least the same priority as any campaign to control GDM. Likewise, other recent large
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Management

paragraphs.text: population studies published by Sheiner et al. observed independent effects of maternal obesity in pregnancy and future offspring morbidities such as cardiovascular,20 infectious,21 and neuropsychiatric (e.g., psychiatric and autism spectrum) disorders,22 and even long-term risks for general childhood malignancies, specifically brain tumors.23
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Management

paragraphs.text: First-line therapy for women with gestational diabetes (GDM-A1) is nutritional and lifestyle modification24; however, the impact on patient outcome has not been conclusively demonstrated in large randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Pharmacotherapy is indicated when nutritional control is inadequate (GDM-A2), especially in patients with elevated fasting glucose levels, as diet is largely ineffective in this metabolic presentation. The ACOG and the ADA recommend insulin as first-line therapy for women in whom the fasting glucose level exceeds 95 mg/dL, the 1-hour postprandial glucose level is greater than 130 to 140 mg/dL, or the 2-hour postprandial glucose level is greater than 120 mg/dL (6.65 mmol/L).1,24 Intermediate- and short-acting insulins served as the first-line therapy for GDM for many years; however, long-acting insulin was approved for use during pregnancy due to its clear advantages in measures of patient compliance. Insulin does not cross the placenta and was classified by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to be “low” risk for use in pregnancy.25 However, it requires multiple daily injections and subsequently the need to train the patients in the technical aspect of treatment, resulting in more weight gain and higher medical costs.26,27 In addition, hypoglycemia occurs in approximately 70% of women who use insulin sometime during their pregnancy.28
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Therefore a safe and effective oral agent for the treatment of gestational diabetes is highly desired. Research efforts have focused on the effectiveness, safety, and placental metabolism of sulfonylurea glyburide, an oral glucose-lowering agent. A meta-analysis of 18 RCTs comparing the efficacy and safety of insulin, metformin, and glyburide26 observed higher infant birth weight, increased incidence of macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia with glyburide. Therefore, despite the rise in use of glyburide in pregnancy, it is not recommended as a first-line therapy in guidelines.1,24,29
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Metformin (Glucophage), another oral glucose-lowering agent, was found to be more acceptable to women than
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: insulin. Metformin demonstrated beneficial effects in terms of controlling glucose levels, limiting gestational weight gain, and fewer episodes of hypoglycemia as compared to insulin for women with GDM.26,30 Although metformin clearly crosses the placenta, it is classified as FDA class B (i.e., animal reproduction studies have failed to demonstrate a risk to the fetus, and there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women) and acceptable as first-line therapy by several professional societies. However, a 2019 meta-analysis examining long-term outcomes found that metforminexposed children appear to experience accelerated postnatal growth, resulting in heavier infants and higher BMI by midchildhood compared to children whose mothers were treated with insulin.31 Further research is needed to establish the role of oral hypoglycemic medications in the treatment of GDM either as a first-line therapy or in addition to insulin.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: GDM is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality in relation to poor glycemic control. In an attempt to reduce the risk of adverse outcome, prenatal surveillance, including assessment of fetal well-being and growth and screening for congenital anomalies, is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Surveillance

paragraphs.text: The timeframe for risk of congenital malformations is during organogenesis, which takes place between 5 and 8 weeks of gestation (3–6 weeks after conception). Therefore prevention of anomalies via improvement of the glycemic profile requires prenatal counseling and adequate compliance during the preconception period, because in the well-controlled population the anomaly rate is similar to that in the general population. However, in poorly controlled pregestational diabetic mothers, the risk is three to five times higher (6%– 12%) (Fig. 17.1).8
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Congenital Anomalies

paragraphs.text: It is believed that GDM does not carry an increased risk of congenital anomalies, because the hyperglycemia
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Congenital Anomalies

paragraphs.text: develops after embryonic organogenesis and the fetus is not exposed to high levels of glucose, ketones, and other metabolites involved in the pathophysiology of malformations in pre-GDM. Nevertheless, women with a history of GDM in previous pregnancies or obesity or those with a presumed diagnosis of pre-GDM (HbA1C levels greater than 9%, fasting glucose levels greater than 120 mg/dL, or GDM diagnosis during the first trimester) may have an increased risk for congenital anomalies and should be offered a detailed sonographic scan for detection of fetal anatomical malformations. Special attention should be focused on the cardiovascular, neural tube, gastrointestinal, urinary, and skeletal systems (Table 17.3) with the possibility of malformation sequences such as VATER or VACTERL (vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheo-esophageal fistulas, renal anomalies, and limb abnormalities).
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Congenital Anomalies

paragraphs.text: Although the detection rate of fetal malformations has its own limitations, the benefits of ultrasonography should be discussed with all patients with GDM, and appropriate multidisciplinary prenatal counseling should be given accordingly to the future parents.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Congenital Anomalies

paragraphs.text: The most common malformations in the fetus of the diabetic mother are cardiac. In addition to developmental malformations, it should be noted that cardiomegaly, septal hypertrophy, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricle outflow tract obstruction may develop; therefore, in cases of poor glycemic control, sequential fetal echocardiograms should be considered.8,32 Caudal agenesis, seen predominantly (300- to 400-fold greater) in insulin-dependent diabetic pregnancies, is a malformation that is specific to the fetus of the diabetic mother.32 The exact etiology of this malformation or the correlation with abnormal glycemic control remains unknown.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Congenital Anomalies

paragraphs.text: The frequency and timing of fetal well-being monitoring are based on the degree of metabolic control, pharmacological intervention, and coexistence of other complications such as
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring Fetal Well-Being

paragraphs.text: hypertension. Generally, antenatal monitoring of women with GDM-A2, as well as those with poor glucose control, should be the same as for women with pre-GDM. A non-stress test and sonographic biophysical profile is suggested to be conducted at least weekly, beginning early in the third trimester.1 However, it should be emphasized that no well-conducted randomized RCTs have defined optimal fetal antenatal management.
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring Fetal Well-Being

paragraphs.text: Virtually all fetuses of GDM mothers are growth promoted. Fetal macrosomia, which is frequently confused with LGA (weight above the 90th percentile for gestational age), is defined as a birth weight greater than 4000 to 4500 g. The incidence of macrosomia increases significantly when the mean maternal blood glucose values are greater than 130 mg/dL. The accuracy of sonographic-estimated weight and characteristics of the fetus of the diabetic mother has been studied quite extensively in the literature because of the increasing incidence of gestational and pregestational diabetes, wide implementation of prenatal diagnosis, and increased awareness of medicolegal issues. Current ultrasound measurement techniques have poor sensitivity and specificity for identifying macrosomic infants. One study found that among women with GDM, the ultrasonography diagnosis of LGA infants resulted in only 22% who were actually LGA at birth.33 A reliable, accurate, and predictive formula based on sonographic data is still lacking; therefore routine sonographic fetal weight assessment to identify fetal macrosomia should be used cautiously in clinical management.
paragraphs.heading: Assessment of Fetal Weight

paragraphs.text: Because the estimated fetal weight is used for risk assessment for labor complications such as obstructed labor and shoulder dystocia, various studies assessed the predictive value of sonographic measures such as the difference between abdominal diameter and biparietal diameter and evaluation of fetal fat layer with quite disappointing results. None of the previously mentioned measures became a tool in the decision-making process regarding mode of delivery (Fig. 17.2).34,35
paragraphs.heading: Assessment of Fetal Weight

paragraphs.text: Polyhydramnios (i.e., increased amniotic fluid volume) is a frequent sonographic finding defined either by a single vertical pocket of 80 mm or according to nomograms of amniotic fluid index per gestational age. The etiologies for polyhydramnios in the context of the fetus of the diabetic mother are the LGA fetus and osmotic diuresis secondary to high glucose level. However, in cases of severe polyhydramnios and poor glycemic control, the presence of malformations such as tracheo-esophageal fistulas, which are more common in the fetus of the diabetic mother, should be considered and investigated appropriately.36 It should be noted that polyhydramnios itself serves as an adjunct sign for fetal macrosomia.
paragraphs.heading: Assessment of Fetal Weight

paragraphs.text: Timing of delivery in pregnancies affected by GDM must weigh the risks of later delivery (stillbirth and delivery complications from excessive fetal growth) versus the potential disadvantage of earlier induction (risks of prematurity, longer labor, and possible increased cesarean delivery). Studies examining the impact of early delivery versus expectant management have yielded conflicting results.37,38 Therefore definite data to support the optimal timing and mode of delivery in women with GDM are lacking. Although earlier deliveries reduce the risk for macrosomia, this policy does not reduce the rate of brachial plexus injuries, clavicular fractures, or neonatal hypoglycemia. Shoulder dystocia may indeed cause debilitating results, and its high frequency in macrosomic fetuses of diabetic mothers leads many clinicians to recommend cesarean rather than vaginal delivery in such cases. Because hundreds of elective cesarean deliveries will be performed to prevent one case of brachial plexus injury, and because the exact cut-off (either 4000 or 4500 g) is controversial, additional data combining maternal and fetal demographic and sonographic parameters are needed for better prediction and risk assessment of shoulder dystocia in the population of macrosomic fetuses of diabetic mothers.
paragraphs.heading: Timing and Mode of Delivery

paragraphs.text: Although patients with GDM-A1 (dietary control) do not require glucose monitoring during labor, women with GDM-A2 require frequent glucose measurements. Most patients are euglycemic during labor and do not require insulin. In the case of hyperglycemia, dextrose solution with intravenous insulin should be administered. The patient should discontinue long-acting insulin treatment during labor and delivery, and regular insulin should be used to meet most or all of the insulin needs of the mother at this time.1
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Management

paragraphs.text: Insulin requirements typically drop markedly after delivery, and most GDM patients do not require insulin postpartum. Up to one-third of affected mothers will have diabetes or impaired glucose metabolism at postpartum screening,1 and up to 70% will develop diabetes (predominantly type 2) later in life.6 Therefore administering OGTTs postpartum and at 3-year intervals is a cost-effective strategy for screening these women. Continuous nutritional modifications to encourage prompt postpartum weight loss, breastfeeding, and moderate exercise are all recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Postpartum Maternal Management

paragraphs.text: In the past, most patients presenting with pregestational diabetes were those affected by juvenile diabetes; however, during recent years, the proportion of maturityonset diabetes of the young has increased in parallel to the increase in maternal age. Pre-GDM is much more difficult to control, and insulin treatment with frequent dosing or by insulin pump is required. Potential risks are the development of life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis on the one hand and profound hypoglycemia on the other. It is recommended that patients and their families should know how to respond quickly and appropriately to hypoglycemia. In contrast to GDM, uncontrolled pre-GDM carries increased risk for fetal malformations. However, the risk of malformations appears to be significantly reduced (to background levels) if the patient conceives when glucose levels are controlled. This can be estimated by the HbA1C. Adequate glucose control near physiologic levels before conception and during pregnancy may reduce the risk of abortion, macrosomia, fetal death, and neonatal morbidity.1
paragraphs.heading: Pregestational Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: Target organ diabetic effects (renal, retinal, cardiac, and nervous system) should be evaluated prior to conception and during pregnancy. The effect of diabetes mellitus on the microvasculature and placenta may cause growth restriction rather than growth promotion, which is the hallmark of GDM.39 Pre-GDM pregnancies are at increased risk for fetal death; therefore fetal movement counting, non-stress testing, and sonographic biophysical profiles performed at appropriate intervals might prove valuable to monitor these pregnancies. Timing and mode of delivery are usually tailored to the patient’s condition, degree of vasculopathy, and fetal thriving, among other factors.
paragraphs.heading: Pregestational Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: The effects of maternal hyperglycemia on the offspring start in utero and can lead to adverse outcomes directly related to maternal glycemic levels during pregnancy both short and long term.40 Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs)
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: are at risk for increased morbidity and even mortality in the neonatal period. Mortality is mostly secondary to malformations and the complications of prematurity. The recognition that there is a clear relationship between degree of control of maternal hyperglycemia and the risk for congenital malformations and the occurrence and severity of birth trauma and neonatal morbidity and mortality has led to improved outcomes.41 Long-term health risks include higher rates of obesity, T2D in childhood, lateonset diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease in adulthood.42,43
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Interestingly, data indicate that in high-resource settings, maternal diabetes is not associated with an increased risk of in-hospital mortality or severe morbidity in very preterm infants with a birth weight of <1500 g.44 However, a new meta-analysis did not find an association in preterm infants <37 weeks’ gestational age between maternal diabetes mellitus and in-hospital mortality or severe neonatal morbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage or cystic periventricular leukomalacia, necrotizing enterocolitis, and retinopathy of prematurity.45
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: As was first postulated in the early 1950s by Pedersen et al.,46 maternal hyperglycemia reaching the fetal circulation increases fetal blood glucose levels, stimulating the fetal pancreas, which results in β-cell hypertrophy and increased insulin secretion. Consequently, there is more transfer to and consumption of glucose in fetal tissue, increasing the glucose gradient between the mother and the fetus, thereby driving more glucose from the maternal to the fetal circulation. This process has been termed the “fetoplacental glucose steal phenomenon” and may explain why some women with fetuses with all the characteristics of diabetic fetopathy are found to have “normal” glucose tolerance.47
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: In pregnancies complicated by T2D, placental protein expression of transporters for glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids is increased, which in turn contributes to increased fetal growth and neonatal adiposity.48 Maternal excess of circulating glucose and other fetal β-cell secretagogues such as lipids and amino acids cross the placenta and stimulate endogenous production of insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1. Because fetal insulin mostly does not cross the placenta, a state of chronic hyperinsulinemia ensues that leads to neonatal complications.49 Insulin is both a growth factor and an anabolic hormone. Thus fetal hyperinsulinemia can result in fetal metabolic reprogramming responsible for short-term problems such as fetal excess growth and/or adiposity due to fat deposition and long-term complications, such as metabolic dysfunction later in life.4,47 Effects include macrosomia; visceromegaly of liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, and heart; or LGA status at birth. These risks are further increased in IDMs due to disproportionate distribution of the fat mass favoring accumulation in the shoulders and abdomen resulting in truncal asymmetry.1,8,33,50
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia caused by maternal diabetes is the most likely cause of stillbirths during the last weeks of pregnancy. Both fetal hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia can independently cause fetal chronic hypoxia by increasing fetal oxygen consumption.51 This, in turn, may contribute to increased risk of metabolic acidosis and birth asphyxia.49 Inverse relationships were identified between cord artery pH and catecholamine levels in IDMs that may contribute to abnormal fetal adaptation to oxygenation and fetal death.52 Neonatal polycythemia was previously explained by the fetal hypoxia-induced increase in erythropoietin production that is related to the control of maternal antepartum hyperglycemia.53 In addition, evidence suggests that increased proportions of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell population in cord blood may possibly be related to altered fetal stem cell mobilization in GDM pregnancies and consequently lead to polycythemia.54
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The hyperviscosity, together with low cardiac output secondary to cardiomyopathy and low maternal levels of protein C, protein S, and antithrombin, contributes to increased risk for thrombotic events, in particular renal vein thrombosis. Increased fetal insulin retards the production and secretion of pulmonary surfactant, leading to increased risk for respiratory distress syndrome up to 38 weeks’ gestation. Fortunately, tighter control of glucose levels in pregnancy significantly reduces the respiratory risks for IDMs.
paragraphs.heading: Implications for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: IDMs are at increased risk for metabolic complications such as hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia in the immediate neonatal period.
paragraphs.heading: Metabolic Problems

paragraphs.text: After birth, the infant is suddenly removed from the source of excess glucose and other nutrients (namely, the mother) but continues to have upregulated insulin production and, despite increased glycogen stores, may be incapable of secreting glucagon and catecholamines to prevent the resultant hypoglycemia. Both the incidence and the severity of hypoglycemia are increased when the mother has received insulin and also when glycemic control has been inadequate. All IDMs require monitoring of blood glucose during the hours and days after birth. Hypoglycemic infants may be asymptomatic or may show clinical signs such as tremor, seizures, poor feeding, respiratory distress, or hypotonia. Debate continues around the definition of hypoglycemia, which is based mostly on statistical calculations and not on the relationship between specific values over specific periods of time and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Although hypoglycemia is self-limited and resolves as the hyperinsulinemia resolves, it may contribute to brain injury if not properly managed.47,50 Unfortunately, medical uncertainty over a condition that may have long-term adverse effects opens the
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: door to litigation in which a judge or jury are left to decide on how low is too low.55
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Congenital malformations in several organ systems are increased two- to threefold in IDMs whose mothers require insulin, but not so in patients with gestational diabetes that developed after the stage of embryogenesis (see Table 17.3). Poor diabetic control with raised HbA1C in the periconceptual period exposes the fetus to hyperglycemia during early embryogenesis and organogenesis, thereby exerting a significant teratogenic effect.57,58 Hyperinsulinemia does not develop until later in pregnancy and therefore does not play a role in this mechanism.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Hypocalcemia is seen in IDMs,56 often after 2 to 3 days of life, and is related to the severity of the maternal diabetes. The mechanisms are related to inadequate parathyroid hormone (PTH), excess calcitonin, and altered vitamin D metabolism. The most common physical sign is tremor, which usually resolves spontaneously, although occasional infants may require calcium supplementation.
paragraphs.heading: Hypocalcemia

paragraphs.text: Neonatal hypomagnesemia is secondary to low maternal levels resulting from increased diuresis and magnesium losses. Hypomagnesemia decreases PTH and responsiveness, leading to hypocalcemia. Correction of hypocalcemia may be non-responsive until hypomagnesemia is corrected.
paragraphs.heading: Hypomagnesemia

paragraphs.text: Later exposure to hyperinsulinemia increases the synthesis and deposition of fat and glycogen in fetal myocardial cells, thereby leading to development of cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy that may lead to functional left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Cardiac dysfunction has a wide range of possible clinical presentations, ranging from an asymptomatic infant to a critically ill infant with either cardiac failure or severe respiratory distress that may be difficult to distinguish from respiratory distress syndrome. The cardiac hypertrophy resolves spontaneously within a few months of birth. Beta blockers slow heart rate, allowing for increased cardiac output and symptomatic improvement. The cardiomyopathy may be recognized in the second trimester by evidence of septal hypertrophy.57–59
paragraphs.heading: Other Novel Challenges

paragraphs.text: Neonatal small left colon syndrome is a rare cause of neonatal intestinal obstruction that is more common in IDMs.60 IDMs are at significantly increased risk for asphyxia for various reasons. Macrosomia increases the risk of adverse outcomes, including shoulder dystocia, brachial plexus injury, and fractures, for the neonate.61 Box 17.1 summarizes the major morbidity in IDMs.
paragraphs.heading: Other Novel Challenges

paragraphs.text: Long-term metabolic effects have been observed in offspring of diabetic mothers and may include increased childhood and adolescent obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, overt diabetes, hypertension, and associated metabolic diseases.18,62–66 In turn, the adult offspring females are more likely to experience diabetes in their own pregnancies, termed the intergenerational cycle of hyperglycemia in pregnancy (Fig. 17.3).67
paragraphs.heading: Other Novel Challenges

paragraphs.text: A meta-analysis of cohort studies of long-term outcome in IDMs identified an increased risk of autism spectrum disorders.68 Likewise, a large Danish cohort found that offspring of mothers with any diabetes diagnosis during pregnancy were at modestly increased risk of developing any psychiatric disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, intellectual disabilities, developmental disorders, and behavioral disorders compared with offspring of mothers without a diabetes diagnosis during pregnancy.69
paragraphs.heading: Other Novel Challenges

paragraphs.text: Breastfeeding should be recommended for its multiple health benefits for the neonate and mother.70–72 It reduces the long-term risk for obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. The inverse association between breastfeeding and obesity is dose dependent (approximately 4% reduction in risk of being overweight per month of breastfeeding) and is seen across all age groups and ethnicities. Children who had been breastfed for at least 2 months also had lower rates of T2D. Because of the increased risk of hypoglycemia in IDMs and the low substrate of breast milk after delivery, hypoglycemia should be monitored and treated accordingly.

17 Pregnancy Complicated by Diabetes Mellitus

### MAYA RAM WEINER, POLINA GUREVICH, ERIC S. SHINWELL, AND YARIV YOGEV

Diabetes mellitus that results from relative or absolute lack of insulin is encountered during pregnancy in two situations: pregestational diabetes mellitus (pre-GDM) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The former refers to women who had diabetes mellitus prior to conception, with microvascular diabetes-associated complications (renal, retinal, cardiac, and nervous system), and the latter refers to otherwise healthy women who developed glucose intolerance during the index pregnancy. These two entities are entirely distinct from both obstetric and neonatal perspectives. Pre-GDM and its associated small vessel injury may affect placental function and fetal growth, whereas GDM is a transient problem that affects the fetus in the opposite way (i.e., macrosomia and its obstetrical consequences—dystocia and increased incidence of operative delivery). This chapter focuses mainly on GDM and its neonatal consequences.

### Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

GDM is one of the most common pregnancy complications. GDM is a state of carbohydrate intolerance that is defined as any degree of hyperglycemia that is recognized for the first time during pregnancy.1 The prevalence of GDM has been increasing over time, generally in parallel with the prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D), possibly due to the increasing rates of obesity in the general population and the trend toward advanced maternal age in pregnancy.2,3 The prevalence has increased by more than 30% in the last two decades3 and is now estimated to affect between 7% and more than 30% of all pregnancies worldwide.3,4 Differences in the geographic location, ethnic groups, and characteristics of the population screened and the diagnostic criteria that are applied are responsible for the wide reported range.3–5 Moreover, and of greater concern, a diagnosis of GDM identifies approximately 80% of these mothers who subsequently develop overt T2D and metabolic syndrome.6 Furthermore, their offspring are also at higher risk for future

T2D, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and future cardiovascular diseases.7

### Screening and Diagnosis

The screening and diagnosis of GDM have a long history of controversy, related mainly to significant implications on health care costs, the effect on obstetric interventions, and whether diagnosis and treatment of GDM will improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. In earlier times, it was common for screening for GDM to be based on the patient’s medical history, focusing on past obstetric outcomes such as bearing a child with macrosomia, and family history of T2D. Those high-risk women underwent a 3-hour, 100-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), and a diagnosis of GDM was established when two or more of the four glucose values met or exceeded threshold levels.1,8 Screening for GDM based on risk factors rather than universal screening was thought to be cost effective and, more importantly, reduced the burden of unnecessary OGTTs in low-risk women. In practice, this approach has complicated the detection process and failed to identify half of the women with GDM who did not have any risk factors.9,10 Realizing the insensitivity of the selective screening, it was suggested first by O’Sullivan et al. in 1973 and later adopted by the US Preventive Services Task Force11 to screen all pregnant women for GDM by a non-fasting, 1-hour, 50-g glucose challenge test (GCT) at or beyond 24 gestational weeks.8 They recommended that only pregnant women who did not pass the GCT should proceed to the second-step, 100-g, 3-hour OGTT for definitive diagnosis.

Consecutive studies suggested that lesser degrees of hyperglycemia are also associated with an increased risk of adverse perinatal outcome, including large for gestational age (LGA) fetuses, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia, cesarean delivery, and hypertensive disorders. Consequently, in 1999, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that a GDM diagnosis should be made similar to

Despite uncertainty regarding the clinical value of treating GDM, data strongly suggest that treatment may reduce adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. ### Treatment

First-line therapy for women with gestational diabetes (GDM-A1) is nutritional and lifestyle modification24; however, the impact on patient outcome has not been conclusively demonstrated in large randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Pharmacotherapy is indicated when nutritional control is inadequate (GDM-A2), especially in patients with elevated fasting glucose levels, as diet is largely ineffective in this metabolic presentation. The ACOG and the ADA recommend insulin as first-line therapy for women in whom the fasting glucose level exceeds 95 mg/dL, the 1-hour postprandial glucose level is greater than 130 to 140 mg/dL, or the 2-hour postprandial glucose level is greater than 120 mg/dL (6.65 mmol/L).1,24 Intermediate- and short-acting insulins served as the first-line therapy for GDM for many years; however, long-acting insulin was approved for use during pregnancy due to its clear advantages in measures of patient compliance. Insulin does not cross the placenta and was classified by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to be “low” risk for use in pregnancy.25 However, it requires multiple daily injections and subsequently the need to train the patients in the technical aspect of treatment, resulting in more weight gain and higher medical costs.26,27 In addition, hypoglycemia occurs in approximately 70% of women who use insulin sometime during their pregnancy.28

Therefore a safe and effective oral agent for the treatment of gestational diabetes is highly desired. Research efforts have focused on the effectiveness, safety, and placental metabolism of sulfonylurea glyburide, an oral glucose-lowering agent. A meta-analysis of 18 RCTs comparing the efficacy and safety of insulin, metformin, and glyburide26 observed higher infant birth weight, increased incidence of macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia with glyburide. Therefore, despite the rise in use of glyburide in pregnancy, it is not recommended as a first-line therapy in guidelines.1,24,29

### Fetal Surveillance

GDM is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality in relation to poor glycemic control. In an attempt to reduce the risk of adverse outcome, prenatal surveillance, including assessment of fetal well-being and growth and screening for congenital anomalies, is recommended.

### Screening for Congenital Anomalies

The timeframe for risk of congenital malformations is during organogenesis, which takes place between 5 and 8 weeks of gestation (3–6 weeks after conception). Therefore prevention of anomalies via improvement of the glycemic profile requires prenatal counseling and adequate compliance during the preconception period, because in the well-controlled population the anomaly rate is similar to that in the general population. However, in poorly controlled pregestational diabetic mothers, the risk is three to five times higher (6%– 12%) (Fig. 17.1).8

It is believed that GDM does not carry an increased risk of congenital anomalies, because the hyperglycemia

Although the detection rate of fetal malformations has its own limitations, the benefits of ultrasonography should be discussed with all patients with GDM, and appropriate multidisciplinary prenatal counseling should be given accordingly to the future parents.

The most common malformations in the fetus of the diabetic mother are cardiac. In addition to developmental malformations, it should be noted that cardiomegaly, septal hypertrophy, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricle outflow tract obstruction may develop; therefore, in cases of poor glycemic control, sequential fetal echocardiograms should be considered.8,32 Caudal agenesis, seen predominantly (300- to 400-fold greater) in insulin-dependent diabetic pregnancies, is a malformation that is specific to the fetus of the diabetic mother.32 The exact etiology of this malformation or the correlation with abnormal glycemic control remains unknown.

### Assessment of Fetal Weight

Virtually all fetuses of GDM mothers are growth promoted. Fetal macrosomia, which is frequently confused with LGA (weight above the 90th percentile for gestational age), is defined as a birth weight greater than 4000 to 4500 g. The incidence of macrosomia increases significantly when the mean maternal blood glucose values are greater than 130 mg/dL. The accuracy of sonographic-estimated weight and characteristics of the fetus of the diabetic mother has been studied quite extensively in the literature because of the increasing incidence of gestational and pregestational diabetes, wide implementation of prenatal diagnosis, and increased awareness of medicolegal issues. Current ultrasound measurement techniques have poor sensitivity and specificity for identifying macrosomic infants. One study found that among women with GDM, the ultrasonography diagnosis of LGA infants resulted in only 22% who were actually LGA at birth.33 A reliable, accurate, and predictive formula based on sonographic data is still lacking; therefore routine sonographic fetal weight assessment to identify fetal macrosomia should be used cautiously in clinical management.

### Timing and Mode of Delivery

Timing of delivery in pregnancies affected by GDM must weigh the risks of later delivery (stillbirth and delivery complications from excessive fetal growth) versus the potential disadvantage of earlier induction (risks of prematurity, longer labor, and possible increased cesarean delivery). Studies examining the impact of early delivery versus expectant management have yielded conflicting results.37,38 Therefore definite data to support the optimal timing and mode of delivery in women with GDM are lacking. Although earlier deliveries reduce the risk for macrosomia, this policy does not reduce the rate of brachial plexus injuries, clavicular fractures, or neonatal hypoglycemia. Shoulder dystocia may indeed cause debilitating results, and its high frequency in macrosomic fetuses of diabetic mothers leads many clinicians to recommend cesarean rather than vaginal delivery in such cases. Because hundreds of elective cesarean deliveries will be performed to prevent one case of brachial plexus injury, and because the exact cut-off (either 4000 or 4500 g) is controversial, additional data combining maternal and fetal demographic and sonographic parameters are needed for better prediction and risk assessment of shoulder dystocia in the population of macrosomic fetuses of diabetic mothers.

### Intrapartum Management

Although patients with GDM-A1 (dietary control) do not require glucose monitoring during labor, women with GDM-A2 require frequent glucose measurements. Most patients are euglycemic during labor and do not require insulin. In the case of hyperglycemia, dextrose solution with intravenous insulin should be administered. The patient should discontinue long-acting insulin treatment during labor and delivery, and regular insulin should be used to meet most or all of the insulin needs of the mother at this time.1

### Postpartum Maternal Management

Insulin requirements typically drop markedly after delivery, and most GDM patients do not require insulin postpartum. Up to one-third of affected mothers will have diabetes or impaired glucose metabolism at postpartum screening,1 and up to 70% will develop diabetes (predominantly type 2) later in life.6 Therefore administering OGTTs postpartum and at 3-year intervals is a cost-effective strategy for screening these women. Continuous nutritional modifications to encourage prompt postpartum weight loss, breastfeeding, and moderate exercise are all recommended.

### Pregestational Diabetes Mellitus

In the past, most patients presenting with pregestational diabetes were those affected by juvenile diabetes; however, during recent years, the proportion of maturityonset diabetes of the young has increased in parallel to the increase in maternal age. Pre-GDM is much more difficult to control, and insulin treatment with frequent dosing or by insulin pump is required. Potential risks are the development of life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis on the one hand and profound hypoglycemia on the other. It is recommended that patients and their families should know how to respond quickly and appropriately to hypoglycemia. In contrast to GDM, uncontrolled pre-GDM carries increased risk for fetal malformations. However, the risk of malformations appears to be significantly reduced (to background levels) if the patient conceives when glucose levels are controlled. This can be estimated by the HbA1C. Adequate glucose control near physiologic levels before conception and during pregnancy may reduce the risk of abortion, macrosomia, fetal death, and neonatal morbidity.1

Target organ diabetic effects (renal, retinal, cardiac, and nervous system) should be evaluated prior to conception and during pregnancy. The effect of diabetes mellitus on the microvasculature and placenta may cause growth restriction rather than growth promotion, which is the hallmark of GDM.39 Pre-GDM pregnancies are at increased risk for fetal death; therefore fetal movement counting, non-stress testing, and sonographic biophysical profiles performed at appropriate intervals might prove valuable to monitor these pregnancies. Timing and mode of delivery are usually tailored to the patient’s condition, degree of vasculopathy, and fetal thriving, among other factors.

### Implications for the Neonate

The effects of maternal hyperglycemia on the offspring start in utero and can lead to adverse outcomes directly related to maternal glycemic levels during pregnancy both short and long term.40 Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs)

are at risk for increased morbidity and even mortality in the neonatal period. Mortality is mostly secondary to malformations and the complications of prematurity. The recognition that there is a clear relationship between degree of control of maternal hyperglycemia and the risk for congenital malformations and the occurrence and severity of birth trauma and neonatal morbidity and mortality has led to improved outcomes.41 Long-term health risks include higher rates of obesity, T2D in childhood, lateonset diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease in adulthood.42,43

Interestingly, data indicate that in high-resource settings, maternal diabetes is not associated with an increased risk of in-hospital mortality or severe morbidity in very preterm infants with a birth weight of <1500 g.44 However, a new meta-analysis did not find an association in preterm infants <37 weeks’ gestational age between maternal diabetes mellitus and in-hospital mortality or severe neonatal morbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage or cystic periventricular leukomalacia, necrotizing enterocolitis, and retinopathy of prematurity.45

As was first postulated in the early 1950s by Pedersen et al.,46 maternal hyperglycemia reaching the fetal circulation increases fetal blood glucose levels, stimulating the fetal pancreas, which results in β-cell hypertrophy and increased insulin secretion. Consequently, there is more transfer to and consumption of glucose in fetal tissue, increasing the glucose gradient between the mother and the fetus, thereby driving more glucose from the maternal to the fetal circulation. This process has been termed the “fetoplacental glucose steal phenomenon” and may explain why some women with fetuses with all the characteristics of diabetic fetopathy are found to have “normal” glucose tolerance.47

In pregnancies complicated by T2D, placental protein expression of transporters for glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids is increased, which in turn contributes to increased fetal growth and neonatal adiposity.48 Maternal excess of circulating glucose and other fetal β-cell secretagogues such as lipids and amino acids cross the placenta and stimulate endogenous production of insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1. Because fetal insulin mostly does not cross the placenta, a state of chronic hyperinsulinemia ensues that leads to neonatal complications.49 Insulin is both a growth factor and an anabolic hormone. Thus fetal hyperinsulinemia can result in fetal metabolic reprogramming responsible for short-term problems such as fetal excess growth and/or adiposity due to fat deposition and long-term complications, such as metabolic dysfunction later in life.4,47 Effects include macrosomia; visceromegaly of liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, and heart; or LGA status at birth. These risks are further increased in IDMs due to disproportionate distribution of the fat mass favoring accumulation in the shoulders and abdomen resulting in truncal asymmetry.1,8,33,50

Chronic intrauterine hypoxia caused by maternal diabetes is the most likely cause of stillbirths during the last weeks of pregnancy. Both fetal hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia can independently cause fetal chronic hypoxia by increasing fetal oxygen consumption.51 This, in turn, may contribute to increased risk of metabolic acidosis and birth asphyxia.49 Inverse relationships were identified between cord artery pH and catecholamine levels in IDMs that may contribute to abnormal fetal adaptation to oxygenation and fetal death.52 Neonatal polycythemia was previously explained by the fetal hypoxia-induced increase in erythropoietin production that is related to the control of maternal antepartum hyperglycemia.53 In addition, evidence suggests that increased proportions of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell population in cord blood may possibly be related to altered fetal stem cell mobilization in GDM pregnancies and consequently lead to polycythemia.54

The hyperviscosity, together with low cardiac output secondary to cardiomyopathy and low maternal levels of protein C, protein S, and antithrombin, contributes to increased risk for thrombotic events, in particular renal vein thrombosis. Increased fetal insulin retards the production and secretion of pulmonary surfactant, leading to increased risk for respiratory distress syndrome up to 38 weeks’ gestation. Fortunately, tighter control of glucose levels in pregnancy significantly reduces the respiratory risks for IDMs.

### Metabolic Problems

IDMs are at increased risk for metabolic complications such as hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia in the immediate neonatal period.

### Hypoglycemia

After birth, the infant is suddenly removed from the source of excess glucose and other nutrients (namely, the mother) but continues to have upregulated insulin production and, despite increased glycogen stores, may be incapable of secreting glucagon and catecholamines to prevent the resultant hypoglycemia. Both the incidence and the severity of hypoglycemia are increased when the mother has received insulin and also when glycemic control has been inadequate. All IDMs require monitoring of blood glucose during the hours and days after birth. Hypoglycemic infants may be asymptomatic or may show clinical signs such as tremor, seizures, poor feeding, respiratory distress, or hypotonia. Debate continues around the definition of hypoglycemia, which is based mostly on statistical calculations and not on the relationship between specific values over specific periods of time and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Although hypoglycemia is self-limited and resolves as the hyperinsulinemia resolves, it may contribute to brain injury if not properly managed.47,50 Unfortunately, medical uncertainty over a condition that may have long-term adverse effects opens the

door to litigation in which a judge or jury are left to decide on how low is too low.55

Congenital malformations in several organ systems are increased two- to threefold in IDMs whose mothers require insulin, but not so in patients with gestational diabetes that developed after the stage of embryogenesis (see Table 17.3). Poor diabetic control with raised HbA1C in the periconceptual period exposes the fetus to hyperglycemia during early embryogenesis and organogenesis, thereby exerting a significant teratogenic effect.57,58 Hyperinsulinemia does not develop until later in pregnancy and therefore does not play a role in this mechanism.

### Hypocalcemia

Hypocalcemia is seen in IDMs,56 often after 2 to 3 days of life, and is related to the severity of the maternal diabetes. The mechanisms are related to inadequate parathyroid hormone (PTH), excess calcitonin, and altered vitamin D metabolism. The most common physical sign is tremor, which usually resolves spontaneously, although occasional infants may require calcium supplementation.

### Hypomagnesemia

Neonatal hypomagnesemia is secondary to low maternal levels resulting from increased diuresis and magnesium losses. Hypomagnesemia decreases PTH and responsiveness, leading to hypocalcemia. Correction of hypocalcemia may be non-responsive until hypomagnesemia is corrected.

### Other Novel Challenges

Later exposure to hyperinsulinemia increases the synthesis and deposition of fat and glycogen in fetal myocardial cells, thereby leading to development of cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy that may lead to functional left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Cardiac dysfunction has a wide range of possible clinical presentations, ranging from an asymptomatic infant to a critically ill infant with either cardiac failure or severe respiratory distress that may be difficult to distinguish from respiratory distress syndrome. The cardiac hypertrophy resolves spontaneously within a few months of birth. Beta blockers slow heart rate, allowing for increased cardiac output and symptomatic improvement. The cardiomyopathy may be recognized in the second trimester by evidence of septal hypertrophy.57–59

Neonatal small left colon syndrome is a rare cause of neonatal intestinal obstruction that is more common in IDMs.60 IDMs are at significantly increased risk for asphyxia for various reasons. Macrosomia increases the risk of adverse outcomes, including shoulder dystocia, brachial plexus injury, and fractures, for the neonate.61 Box 17.1 summarizes the major morbidity in IDMs.

### Breastfeeding in Women With Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

Breastfeeding should be recommended for its multiple health benefits for the neonate and mother.70–72 It reduces the long-term risk for obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. The inverse association between breastfeeding and obesity is dose dependent (approximately 4% reduction in risk of being overweight per month of breastfeeding) and is seen across all age groups and ethnicities. Because of the increased risk of hypoglycemia in IDMs and the low substrate of breast milk after delivery, hypoglycemia should be monitored and treated accordingly.
